text: After Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea, in the days of King Herod, wise men from the east came to Jerusalem

footnotes.text: The Greek opens with a genitive absolute construction ("Jesus having been born"), which sets the scene rather than narrating the birth itself; the rendering "After Jesus was born" preserves that background function and keeps the sentence moving toward the main clause, the arrival of the visitors. The Greek word magoi has no exact English equivalent: "wise men" is used here because it is familiar to the ear and avoids the misleading overtones of "magicians" or "sorcerers," while "astrologers" would be more precise about their craft and "Magi" would simply transliterate the term. Their number is never stated; the traditional three comes from the three gifts in verse 11, not from the text. The phrase "in the days of King Herod" translates a Semitic-flavored time expression literally, since the rhythm of "in the days of" reads well aloud; "during the reign of Herod the king" would be an equally faithful but flatter alternative. Note also that the sentence continues into verse 2 without a full stop, matching the single flowing sentence of the Greek.

Magos is a loanword from Old Persian, originally denoting a member of the priestly caste of the Medes, and by the first century used broadly for practitioners of astrology, dream interpretation, and esoteric learning. The word could carry a negative charge in Greek writing (compare its use of Simon and Elymas elsewhere in the New Testament), which makes Matthew's positive portrayal striking. The phrase apo anatolōn is plural, literally "from risings," that is, from where the sun rises — hence "from the east"; in the next verse the same root appears in the singular of the star's rising, a deliberate echo. "Bethlehem of Judea" distinguishes this village from another Bethlehem in Galilee, in the territory of Zebulun.

Herod the Great ruled as Rome's client king over Judea from about 37 to 4 BC, an able builder (the expanded temple was his work) and a ruler notorious for eliminating perceived rivals, including members of his own family. His reign anchors the birth of Jesus before 4 BC. Bethlehem was a small village roughly six miles south of Jerusalem, remembered as the hometown of David. Astral observation was highly developed in Babylon and Persia, and the ancient world widely assumed that celestial events could signal the birth of a ruler; Roman writers record an expectation in the east that a world ruler would arise from Judea. A delegation of eastern dignitaries traveling to honor a king would have been a recognizable, politically charged event.

Matthew opens his account of Jesus' childhood with foreigners who read the heavens seeking a Jewish king, while Jerusalem's own leadership will be troubled by the news. This frames a theme that runs to the Gospel's final verse: the nations coming to worship the Messiah. Readers have long heard echoes of the promises that Gentiles would come to the light and bring gifts, and of the pagan seer Balaam who spoke of a star rising out of Jacob. The episode also raises the perennial question of how God may use knowledge outside Israel's covenant — here the sciences of the east — to lead people to Christ, without endorsing astrology as such.

The text of this verse is remarkably stable across the manuscript tradition. Minor variation involves word order and the spelling of Bethlehem, and some witnesses omit or vary the article with "Herod the king," none of which affects the sense.

This verse begins the Gospel reading for Epiphany, celebrated on January 6 in the West and closely associated with the Theophany season in the East, where in many traditions the visit of the Magi is commemorated with the Nativity. It is among the most widely used Gospel texts in Christmas services, processions, and hymnody.

text: and asked, "Where is the one who has been born king of the Jews? We saw his star when it rose, and we have come to worship him."

footnotes.text: The Greek opens with the participle λέγοντες, "saying," continuing the sentence begun in verse 1; since English resists a long run-on, the participle is rendered as a finite verb, "and asked," which also signals that a question follows. The phrase ὁ τεχθεὶς βασιλεὺς τῶν Ἰουδαίων is literally "the born king of the Jews"; the rendering "the one who has been born king of the Jews" preserves the passive participle and the emphatic word order, which stresses that this king holds his title by birth. An alternative rendering is "the one who has been born to be king of the Jews." The clause ἐν τῇ ἀνατολῇ can be taken either spatially, "in the east," or temporally, "at its rising" — the technical astronomical sense of a star's first appearance above the horizon. The temporal sense, "when it rose," is adopted here because the noun stands in the singular with the article, unlike the plural ἀπὸ ἀνατολῶν ("from the east") in verse 1. Finally, προσκυνῆσαι is rendered "to worship"; "to pay homage" or "to do obeisance" are equally defensible.

ἀνατολή comes from ἀνατέλλω, "to rise up, spring up," used of the sun, stars, and even of shoots from a root. The same root gives the noun both meanings that hover over this verse: the direction of sunrise (the east) and the act of rising. The verb προσκυνέω is built from πρός ("toward") and κυνέω ("to kiss"), and originally described blowing or throwing a kiss toward a superior, then prostration before a king or a god. In Greek the participle τεχθείς is aorist passive of τίκτω, "to give birth," the same verb used in the birth announcements of chapter 1.

"King of the Jews" was the very title Herod the Great held by decree of the Roman senate, which is why the question is politically explosive and why verse 3 reports his alarm. Astrologers from Persia or Babylon — the μάγοι were originally a priestly caste associated with dream interpretation and star-lore — were widely believed to read the births and deaths of rulers in the sky. Ancient sources record the appearance of new stars, comets, and planetary conjunctions being interpreted as heralding royal births, and Roman writers describe a well-known expedition of eastern magi who came west to honor an emperor. Whatever the astronomical phenomenon, the narrative assumes a world where the heavens announce a change of thrones.

The first people in this Gospel to seek out and worship the newborn Messiah are foreigners, not Israelites — a quiet foreshadowing of the closing commission to make disciples of all nations. The verb translated "worship" is used throughout this Gospel both for reverence toward a human superior and for the worship due to God alone; the narrator lets the ambiguity stand, but the reader who knows the child is "God with us" hears more in it than the magi themselves may have intended. The title "king of the Jews" appears again only at the end of the Gospel, on the placard above the cross, framing the whole story between the homage of Gentiles and the mockery of soldiers.

The wording of this verse is unusually stable across the manuscript tradition. Notably, the singular ἐν τῇ ἀνατολῇ here is uniformly attested and stands in deliberate contrast to the plural ἀπὸ ἀνατολῶν in verse 1, which supports reading the singular in its technical sense of a star's rising rather than simply as a geographical direction.

This passage is read at the feast of Epiphany, celebrated on the sixth of January in most traditions, which commemorates the manifestation of Christ to the nations. The question "Where is the one who has been born king of the Jews?" and the star that guides the seekers have shaped centuries of Epiphany hymnody, processions, and the custom of blessing homes with the initials of the traditional names of the magi.

text: When King Herod heard this, he was deeply disturbed, and all Jerusalem with him.

footnotes.text: The Greek says only "when he heard"; "this" is supplied so the sentence stands on its own when read aloud. The verb rendered "was deeply disturbed" (etarachthē) is a passive form meaning "was stirred up, agitated, thrown into turmoil" — alternatives include "was troubled," "was alarmed," or "was shaken." "Deeply" carries the force of a word used elsewhere for water churned up or a heart in anguish, without adding a new idea. The second clause has no verb in Greek (literally "and all Jerusalem with him"), and the translation keeps that terse echo rather than repeating the verb, since the shorter line reads better and preserves the original's clipped effect. "All Jerusalem" renders a collective expression; some render it "all the people of Jerusalem," but the city-as-a-whole phrasing is closer to the Greek and stronger in the ear.

The verb tarassō is used of water being stirred or troubled, and in the Gospels of deep inner agitation — Jesus himself is "troubled" in spirit by grief and by the shadow of the cross. It is not merely intellectual puzzlement but visceral upheaval. The name for Jerusalem here appears as a feminine singular (pasa Hierosolyma), an unusual form since this Gospel elsewhere treats the name as a neuter plural; the feminine suggests the city is being thought of as a single personified whole, as a mother-city. Note too that the singular verb agrees with Herod alone, with the city joined afterward by the phrase "with him" — grammatically the turmoil radiates outward from the throne.

Manuscripts differ in the word order of the royal title: some read "the king, Herod," others "Herod the king," and a few omit the article. The sense is unaffected either way, and no translation decision hangs on the variant.

Herod the Great, an Idumean by descent, was granted the title "king of the Jews" by Rome and ruled Judea from 37 to 4 BC. He was a spectacular builder — the temple, Caesarea, Masada — and notoriously suspicious of rivals, executing his wife Mariamne, her relatives, and three of his own sons on suspicion of conspiracy. Jerusalem's dread is therefore realistic: the city had learned what happened when Herod felt his throne threatened. Since he held the very title the magi used, the report of a newborn "king of the Jews" struck at the legitimacy of his dynasty.

The verse sets up the Gospel's deep irony: the birth of the true king brings joy to foreigners who travel from afar, but panic to the reigning king and the holy city itself. Jerusalem, which should have welcomed its Messiah, is instead "troubled" — a note that returns at the end of the Gospel, when the same city hands over the same "king of the Jews" to death. The contrast between Gentile worship and the capital's fear anticipates the wider movement of the Gospel toward all nations.

This verse belongs to the Epiphany narrative and is read in that season alongside the visit of the magi, where the church hears both the homage of the nations and the resistance of earthly power in a single account.

text: So he called together all the chief priests and scribes of the people and asked them where the Messiah was to be born.

versions.text: He gathered all the chief priests and scribes of the people and inquired of them where the Messiah was to be born.
versions.explanation: For oral reading, "called together" reads more naturally than "gathered" with people as the object, and "asked them" is smoother than the formal "inquired of them." Beginning with "So" renders the connective force of καί and links the verse to Herod's disturbance in the previous verse.

footnotes.text: The opening καί is rendered "So" rather than "And," since it carries a consequential force here: Herod's alarm in the previous verse leads directly to this action. The verb ἐπυνθάνετο is an imperfect, suggesting a sustained or repeated inquiry; it could be rendered "kept asking" or "began to question them," but the simple "asked" preserves the narrative pace for reading aloud. The Greek ὁ χριστός is a title with the definite article, "the Anointed One," and is here given as "the Messiah" rather than "the Christ," because in Herod's mouth it is not a name for Jesus but a reference to the expected deliverer. The present tense γεννᾶται (literally "is born") functions as a general or anticipatory present — the question is where Scripture says the Messiah is to be born — hence "was to be born" in this past-tense narrative.

συναγαγών, "having gathered together," is from the same root as συναγωγή, "assembly, synagogue" — Herod convenes a formal consultation. γραμματεῖς means literally "men of letters," experts in the written Law; the qualifier τοῦ λαοῦ ("of the people") in Greek stands after the pair and may govern both nouns, so that the whole body is presented as the official leadership of Israel. πυνθάνομαι is a verb of careful inquiry, used of seeking information from those who know.

The "chief priests" were the priestly aristocracy of Jerusalem — the serving high priest together with former high priests and heads of the leading priestly families who oversaw the temple. The "scribes" were the trained interpreters of the Law. Together these groups made up the core of the ruling council, and Herod, an Idumean whose claim to the throne rested on Roman favor rather than Davidic descent, had every political reason to be anxious about a rival "king of the Jews." Consulting the recognized authorities on Scripture was the natural way to locate a messianic prophecy.

Herod's question presupposes a widespread expectation that the Messiah's birthplace was fixed by prophecy. The scene carries a deep irony that runs through this Gospel: the religious authorities can cite the text correctly yet do not act on it, while foreign visitors travel far to worship. The gathering of "all the chief priests and scribes" against the newborn king also foreshadows the later assemblies of these same offices that will oppose him.

The wording of this verse is stable in the manuscript tradition. Some witnesses add the article before "scribes," which would present the priests and scribes as two distinct bodies rather than as one convened assembly; the sense is scarcely affected.

text: They told him, "In Bethlehem of Judea, for this is what was written through the prophet:

versions.text: They told him, "In Bethlehem of Judea, for this is what the prophet has written:
versions.explanation: The Greek γέγραπται διὰ τοῦ προφήτου is a divine passive: the writing comes through the prophet, not from him as the ultimate author. 'The prophet has written' makes the prophet the agent and loses the sense that God speaks through him. 'What was written through the prophet' preserves this while reading just as smoothly aloud.

footnotes.text: The Greek opens with «οἱ δὲ εἶπαν αὐτῷ», literally "and they said to him." Rendered here as "They told him" — the small connective δέ, which simply marks the shift back to the other speakers, is carried by the sentence rhythm rather than by an added "and" or "but," which would slow the reading aloud. The perfect verb γέγραπται ("it has been written and so stands written") is given as "this is what was written"; other defensible renderings are "for so it is written" or "for thus it stands written." The English keeps the quotation open at the end of the verse with a colon, so that the prophetic citation in the following verse is heard as the continuation of the scribes' answer, spoken in one breath.

γέγραπται is a perfect passive — a standard formula for citing Scripture, stressing not the past act of writing but the abiding validity of what was written. The passive is a "divine passive": God is the unnamed writer. The preposition διά with the genitive ("through the prophet") marks intermediate agency: the prophet is the channel, not the ultimate source. The verb form εἶπαν shows the Hellenistic tendency to give aorists the first-aorist ending -αν in place of the classical εἶπον.

"Bethlehem of Judea" is specified because a second Bethlehem lay in the territory of Zebulun in the north (Joshua 19:15). The Judean Bethlehem sat roughly six miles south of Jerusalem and was remembered above all as the home town of David and the setting of the story of Ruth. The chief priests and scribes answer immediately and without hesitation: the expectation that the Messiah would be born there was common knowledge among the learned of the day.

The bulk of the manuscript tradition reads simply "through the prophet," leaving the source unnamed even though the words that follow come from Micah. A small number of witnesses supply the name, reading "through Micah the prophet," almost certainly a later clarifying addition rather than the original wording. There is also minor variation between the Hellenistic form εἶπαν and the classical εἶπον, with no difference in meaning.

The unnamed prophet speaks, but the writing is God's; the formula treats Scripture as one continuous divine word delivered through many human voices. There is a sharp irony in the scene: those who can locate the Messiah's birthplace from memory take no step toward it, while foreigners guided only by a star make the journey. Knowledge of the text, the Gospel implies, is not the same as coming to worship.

text: 'And you, Bethlehem, in the land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah; for out of you will come a ruler who will shepherd my people Israel.'"

footnotes.text: The quotation blends Micah 5:2 with a phrase from 2 Samuel 5:2, and the wording here differs from both the Hebrew and the standard Greek versions of Micah. Where Micah says Bethlehem is 'little to be among the clans of Judah,' this citation reverses the sense: 'by no means least.' The translation keeps that emphatic negative, since the Greek οὐδαμῶς is a strong 'not at all,' rather than smoothing it toward the prophet's original wording. 'In the land of Judah' renders the simple apposition γῆ Ἰούδα, which literally reads 'land of Judah' standing alongside 'Bethlehem'; adding 'in the' keeps the line readable aloud without breaking its rhythm. ἡγεμόσιν could be rendered 'rulers,' 'leaders,' or 'governors'; 'rulers' was chosen to echo the related word ἡγούμενος ('a ruler') in the second half of the verse, preserving the link the Greek makes between the city's rank and the leader who comes from it. The single closing quotation mark ends the prophet's words; the double mark ends the chief priests' answer to Herod begun in verse 5.

The Hebrew of Micah reads 'thousands' (clans, military units) where the Greek here has ἡγεμόσιν, 'rulers' — the two Hebrew words differ only in vowel pointing, so the citation may reflect a known alternate reading rather than a loose paraphrase. ποιμανεῖ is future of ποιμαίνω, 'to shepherd, to tend a flock,' a verb that in Greek political language also means 'to govern.' The pairing of ἡγούμενος (leader) with ποιμανεῖ (will shepherd) sets rule and care side by side in one image.

Bethlehem was David's hometown, and the shepherd language deliberately recalls the words spoken to David at his anointing: 'you shall shepherd my people Israel.' Naming a small village as the birthplace of the ruler underlines a recurring biblical pattern in which God's choice falls on what is overlooked. Calling Israel 'my people' places the speaker as God himself, so the promised ruler exercises a shepherding that belongs to God — a point later Christian reading connected to Jesus' self-description as the good shepherd.

Bethlehem lay about six miles south of Jerusalem, a modest agricultural settlement of perhaps a few hundred people. That Herod's scholars could answer his question instantly shows how firmly this expectation was fixed in learned Jewish tradition of the period. For Herod, an Idumean ruling by Roman appointment and famously anxious about rivals, the announcement of a Davidic ruler born in David's own town was a direct political threat — which explains his secret summons in the next verse.
This verse belongs to the traditional readings for Christmas and Epiphany, and its lines are widely echoed in carols and hymns celebrating the small town chosen for the Messiah's birth.

text: Then Herod called the wise men to him in secret and found out from them the exact time the star had appeared.

footnotes.text: The single Greek verb ἠκρίβωσεν means "to determine with precision," and English needs a phrase to carry it: "found out from them the exact time." Older renderings say "inquired diligently" or "ascertained," but the Greek stresses the result (he got the precise information), not merely the effort. The participial construction (literally "having secretly called the wise men, he determined...") is unpacked into two coordinated clauses, "called... and found out," which reads far more naturally aloud. "In secret" is placed after "called the wise men to him" so the sentence lands on the sinister note rather than burying it. The Greek phrase τοῦ φαινομένου ἀστέρος uses a present participle, literally "of the appearing star" — that is, the star that had been showing itself; English idiom requires a finite clause, hence "the time the star had appeared." Some render it "the time when the star appeared" or "how long the star had been visible," and either sense fits. "Wise men" translates μάγοι; "magi" is a common alternative that keeps the foreign flavor, while "astrologers" captures their craft but sounds pejorative in modern English.

ἀκριβόω is a rare verb, occurring in the New Testament only here and in verse 16, where the same root reappears in the phrase "the time he had determined exactly from the wise men." The related adverb ἀκριβῶς turns up in the very next verse, where Herod tells the men to "search carefully." The repetition of this precision-word three times in a few lines is deliberate: Herod is meticulous, and his meticulousness is deadly. λάθρᾳ is a dative form used adverbially, "secretly, without others knowing"; the same word describes Joseph's plan to divorce Mary quietly in 1:19, though there the secrecy is merciful rather than murderous. μάγοι originally denoted a priestly caste among the Medes and Persians and came to cover astrologers and dream-interpreters generally.

Herod the Great ruled Judea as a client king of Rome from 37 to 4 BC. Ancient sources portray a ruler obsessed with plots against his throne, who executed his wife Mariamne, her grandfather, and three of his own sons. A secret interview with foreign visitors about a rival king fits everything known of him. Astrologers in the Babylonian and Persian world kept dated records of celestial phenomena, so the question about timing is exactly what one would ask such men, and they would be able to answer it. The chronological detail matters for the narrative: on the basis of what he learns here, Herod later sets the age limit for the children of Bethlehem at two years and under.

The secrecy is the first sign that Herod's later profession of a desire to worship is a lie. Two kinds of seeking stand side by side in this chapter: the foreigners who travel far to bow down, and the reigning king who hides in his palace and plots. Matthew presents Herod as a new Pharaoh, threatened by a child and moving toward the slaughter of infants, and the whole episode prepares for the flight to Egypt and the exodus pattern that follows. There is deep irony in the fact that Herod alone acts on the prophecy he has just heard, yet acts to destroy the one it promises.

The wording of this verse is unusually stable across the manuscript tradition. A handful of witnesses vary the word order of the closing phrase, reading "of the star that was appearing" with the article repeated, but the sense is unaffected and no translation difference results.

This verse belongs to the Gospel reading for Epiphany, celebrated on January 6, which commemorates the visit of the wise men and the manifestation of Christ to the nations. In many traditions the whole passage of verses 1 through 12 is read, so that Herod's plotting is heard within the same reading as the offering of gold, frankincense, and myrrh.

text: So he sent them to Bethlehem and said, "Go and search carefully for the child. When you have found him, bring me word, so that I too may go and worship him."

versions.text: He sent them to Bethlehem and said, "Go and search carefully for the child. When you have found him, report to me, so that I too may go and worship him."
versions.explanation: Two small improvements for oral flow and accuracy: adding "So" links the participial clause (πέμψας) to the preceding verse's action naturally in spoken English; and "bring me word" renders ἀπαγγείλατέ μοι more idiomatically and with better rhythm than the flat, bureaucratic-sounding "report to me."

footnotes.text: The Greek imperative pair ἐξετάσατε ἀκριβῶς means literally "inquire accurately" or "make exact investigation"; the rendering "search carefully" keeps the sense while reading smoothly aloud. The opening participle Πορευθέντες ("having gone") is idiomatically rendered as a simple "Go and…", a common Semitic-flavored construction in this Gospel. ἀπαγγείλατέ μοι is literally "report back to me"; "bring me word" preserves the flavor of a royal command without sounding bureaucratic. The final clause ὅπως κἀγὼ ἐλθὼν προσκυνήσω αὐτῷ is purpose ("so that I too may…"), and the emphatic κἀγώ ("I also") is caught by "I too". The verse opens with καὶ πέμψας ("and having sent"), rendered "So he sent them" to keep the narrative momentum from the previous verse.

ἀκριβῶς ("exactly, accurately") echoes the verb ἠκρίβωσεν in verse 7, where Herod "ascertained exactly" the time of the star. The repetition of the same root ties the two verses together: Herod is precise about the timing and demands precision about the place. προσκυνέω, translated "worship", means to prostrate oneself, and could describe homage paid to a king as well as reverence toward God — a deliberate ambiguity in the narrative. παιδίον is the diminutive of παῖς, "little child", used consistently for Jesus throughout this chapter rather than βρέφος ("infant").

Herod's words are a lie in the mouth of a man who intends murder (see verse 16). The irony is sharp: the same verb of worship that the wise men will genuinely perform in verse 11 is here used deceitfully. Early commentators noted that Herod, though scheming, unwittingly serves the divine purpose by sending the magi toward Bethlehem, the very town named by the prophets. The passage raises the question of outward religious language used as a mask for hostility to God's purposes.

Bethlehem lay about eight kilometers (five miles) south of Jerusalem, an easy journey of a few hours. Herod the Great, an Idumean ruler installed by Rome, was notoriously suspicious of rivals and had already executed members of his own family. He could easily have sent soldiers or officials to accompany the magi; using foreign visitors as unwitting informants fits his known pattern of relying on covert intelligence. The secrecy of verse 7 continues here: the inquiry is private, not a state mission.

The word order of the command varies in the manuscript tradition: some witnesses read ἐξετάσατε ἀκριβῶς ("search carefully"), others ἀκριβῶς ἐξετάσατε ("carefully search"). The difference is stylistic only and does not affect the meaning or the translation.

This verse belongs to the Gospel reading for Epiphany, the celebration of the manifestation of Christ to the nations. In the liturgical telling, Herod's false promise of worship stands in stark contrast to the genuine adoration of the magi that follows, a contrast often drawn out in Epiphany preaching.

text: After they had heard the king, they set out; and behold, the star they had seen at its rising went ahead of them until it stopped over the place where the child was.

versions.text: So they set out, and the star they had seen when it rose went ahead of them until it stopped over the place where the child was.
versions.explanation: Two elements of the Greek are dropped: the participial clause ἀκούσαντες τοῦ βασιλέως ("having heard the king"), which links their departure to Herod's instruction, and the attention-marker καὶ ἰδού ("and behold"), which heightens the narrative and reads well aloud. Rendering ἐν τῇ ἀνατολῇ as "at its rising" also keeps the astronomical sense consistent with verse 2.

footnotes.text: "At its rising" renders ἐν τῇ ἀνατολῇ, the same phrase used in verse 2. The noun ἀνατολή can mean either the compass direction ("the east") or the act of a heavenly body rising above the horizon. Since the singular with the article is the standard astronomical idiom for a star's rising, and since the magi came from the east themselves, "at its rising" is preferred here; "in the east" remains a defensible alternative. "Behold" keeps the narrative marker καὶ ἰδού, which invites the hearer to look with the magi; some renderings drop it as archaic, but read aloud it carries the sudden wonder of the moment. The Greek οὗ ἦν τὸ παιδίον is literally "where the child was"; "over the place where the child was" makes the spatial sense explicit for the ear without adding information. Note also that Greek παιδίον means a young child, not a newborn infant (βρέφος).

προῆγεν is imperfect — "kept going ahead of them" — expressing continuous motion, while ἐστάθη is aorist passive, a single decisive halt: "came and stood." The contrast of tenses gives the sentence its shape: sustained movement resolving into stillness. ἀκούσαντες τοῦ βασιλέως uses the genitive after ἀκούω, which can carry the nuance of heeding as well as merely hearing. The redundant participle ἐλθών ("having come, it stood") is a Semitic-flavored idiom common in this Gospel and usually left untranslated in English.

Some manuscripts read ἔστη (aorist active, "stood") rather than ἐστάθη (aorist passive, "was made to stand"). The passive form, which has the stronger attestation, may hint that the star was halted by divine agency rather than stopping of itself, though in Hellenistic Greek this passive is often simply intransitive in force.

Ancient readers understood celestial phenomena as signs attending the birth or death of great figures, and court astrologers in the Persian and Babylonian world watched for such omens. A star's "rising" (its first visibility above the eastern horizon after a period of invisibility) was a technically significant event in ancient astronomy. Proposals for the phenomenon behind the account have included a planetary conjunction, a comet, and a nova; the narrative itself shows no interest in a natural explanation, and the star's guiding of travelers to a specific house resists ordinary astronomy.

The star's leading fulfills a pattern found throughout Scripture in which God guides his people by a visible sign, as with the pillar of cloud and fire in the wilderness. That Gentile seekers are led by the heavens while Jerusalem's scribes, who possessed the Scriptures, stay behind is a deliberate irony in this Gospel: revelation reaches those who follow the light they are given. Interpreters have long debated whether the star is a natural phenomenon providentially timed or an angelic or wholly miraculous light; the text's emphasis falls not on its nature but on its purpose — to bring the nations to worship.

This verse belongs to the Gospel reading for Epiphany, the celebration of Christ's manifestation to the nations, and the image of the guiding star has shaped the season's hymnody and processional customs across many traditions.

text: When they saw the star, they rejoiced with exceedingly great joy.

versions.text: When they saw the star, they were overwhelmed with joy.
versions.explanation: The Greek piles up intensifiers ("they rejoiced a great joy exceedingly"), and "overwhelmed with joy" flattens the emphatic triple construction, dropping the force of σφόδρα. Retaining the cognate verb-noun pairing with the intensifier preserves the emphasis and still reads smoothly aloud.

footnotes.text: The Greek reads literally "they rejoiced a great joy exceedingly," a construction that piles up intensifiers: the verb, its cognate noun, an adjective ("great"), and an adverb ("exceedingly"). English cannot easily reproduce the doubled noun-and-verb, so the rendering keeps the redundancy in adjectival form: "rejoiced with exceedingly great joy." Alternatives such as "were overjoyed," "were filled with tremendous joy," or "rejoiced with very great joy" are all defensible; the chosen wording preserves the deliberate excess of the original and gives the line a rising cadence when read aloud. The participle "seeing" is rendered as a temporal clause, "When they saw," since the sighting is what triggers the joy.

ἐχάρησαν χαρὰν μεγάλην is a cognate (internal) accusative — the verb takes a noun of the same root as its object — a figure common in Hebrew and Aramaic and frequent in the Greek of the Septuagint, where it often translates an infinitive absolute. Matthew's Greek here has a distinctly Semitic ring. The adverb σφόδρα ("very, exceedingly") then stacks a fourth layer of emphasis on top of μεγάλην; the effect is close to a superlative, roughly "they were overwhelmed with joy." The verb χαίρω and the noun χαρά belong to the same word family as χάρις, "grace/favor."

This is the first outburst of joy in Matthew's Gospel, and it belongs to foreigners rather than to Jerusalem, which is troubled (2:3). The joy is occasioned by the reappearing star, but its object is the child it leads to; interpreters have long read the verse as a picture of the response of the nations to the revelation of the Messiah. The extravagant piling up of terms marks the moment as more than ordinary relief at finding the way: it is the joy of arrival at the goal of a long search, anticipating the worship of the next verse.

Ancient travelers navigated by celestial observation, and Greco-Roman as well as Babylonian astrological tradition read the appearance of new stars as announcing the birth of rulers. For observers trained in such reading of the heavens, the star's halting over a particular place would confirm that their long journey and their interpretation had been vindicated — hence the intensity of the reaction described here.

The wording of this verse is unusually stable across the manuscript tradition, with only minor variation in the placement of the intensifier and in spelling. Some witnesses read the aorist participle in a slightly different form, but no variant affects the sense.

The verse belongs to the Gospel reading for Epiphany, where the joy of the star-gazers is traditionally taken up in the festal hymns and antiphons celebrating the manifestation of Christ to the nations.

text: And when they came into the house, they saw the child with Mary his mother, and they fell down and worshiped him. Then they opened their treasures and offered him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh.

versions.text: Going into the house, they saw the child with Mary his mother, and they fell down and worshiped him. Then they opened their treasures and presented him with gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh.
versions.explanation: Two small refinements for oral flow and accuracy: restoring the connective 'And' at the opening (Greek καί) with a finite clause ('when they came into the house') reads more smoothly aloud than the participial 'Going into the house'; and 'offered him gifts' renders προσήνεγκαν αὐτῷ δῶρα more directly than 'presented him with gifts', while avoiding the slight awkwardness of the colon following 'with gifts'.

footnotes.text: The verse is built as a chain of Greek clauses joined by «and» (καί), with three participles — «having come», «having fallen», «having opened». Strict imitation of this would produce a breathless run-on in English, so the chain is broken into two sentences, and the third «and» is rendered «Then», which keeps the forward motion of the narrative while giving a reader breath. «They fell down and worshiped him» renders the participle πεσόντες plus the finite verb προσεκύνησαν as two coordinated actions, since «falling, they worshiped» is stilted aloud; the sense is a single gesture of prostration. A colon introduces the list of gifts, where the Greek simply apposes them; alternatives such as «gifts of gold, frankincense, and myrrh» blur the fact that «gifts» and the three items stand side by side in the Greek. «Treasures» keeps the ambiguity of θησαυρούς, which may mean either the valuables themselves or the chests that held them; «treasure chests» or «coffers» would be equally defensible.

τὸ παιδίον, «the child», is a diminutive of παῖς and is not the word for a newborn (βρέφος, used in the Bethlehem shepherd account elsewhere); it covers a toddler as readily as an infant. προσκυνέω literally pictures moving toward and kissing — the gesture of an inferior before a superior — and covers everything from court etiquette to the worship of God; the added πεσόντες («having fallen») marks it here as full prostration to the ground. Note that Matthew has already used the same verb on Herod's lips as a pretense, so the word carries an ironic echo. θησαυρός is the root behind English «thesaurus», a storehouse of things laid up.

«The house» (οἰκία), not a stable or a feeding trough, and «the child» rather than «the infant» suggest that some time has passed since the birth — consistent with Herod's later calculation of two years. The three commodities are luxury trade goods: gold, and two aromatic resins tapped from trees in southern Arabia and the Horn of Africa and carried north along the incense routes. Frankincense was burned as incense in temple worship; myrrh was used in perfume, in medicine, and in preparing bodies for burial. Such gifts are exactly what envoys from the east would carry when approaching a royal court. The text never states how many visitors there were; the traditional number three is inferred from the three gifts.

The prostration of foreign dignitaries before a Judean child is Matthew's opening statement that this king's reign reaches beyond Israel. Interpreters have long read the gifts symbolically — gold for kingship, frankincense for divinity or priesthood, myrrh foreshadowing burial and the passion — though the text itself offers no such commentary and some read them simply as royal tribute. Mary is named while Joseph is absent from the scene, which readers have connected to Matthew's account of the virginal conception. Whether προσεκύνησαν here means adoration owed to God or homage owed to a king is debated; Matthew's Gospel elsewhere presses the word toward worship in the fullest sense.

Some witnesses read «they found» (εὗρον) instead of «they saw» (εἶδον), likely a scribal smoothing after the search motif of the preceding verses; the better-attested reading is «they saw». There is also minor variation in the order of «Mary his mother» versus «his mother Mary» in a few manuscripts and versions. Neither variant affects the sense.

This verse stands at the heart of the feast of Epiphany, celebrated on 6 January in the West and connected with the Theophany in Eastern usage; it is read as the manifestation of Christ to the nations. The scene is one of the most frequently depicted in Christian art and hymnody, and the offering of the gifts has shaped the custom of gift-giving in the Christmas season.

text: And having been warned in a dream not to go back to Herod, they returned to their own country by another route.

footnotes.text: The Greek χρηματισθέντες is a passive participle with no stated agent — literally "having been divinely instructed/warned." The translation supplies "warned" because the content of the message is a prohibition, and leaves the agent unnamed, as the Greek does; the passive here is understood as a reverent way of saying God acted. Some render it "having been divinely warned" to make the source explicit, but that adds weight the sentence does not carry aloud. The phrase κατ' ὄναρ ("in a dream") is placed immediately after "warned" to keep the rhythm of the clause intact. For δι' ἄλλης ὁδοῦ, "by another route" is preferred over "by another way" or "by another road": "way" is ambiguous in English (manner versus path), and "route" reads cleanly in oral delivery. ἀνεχώρησαν, "they withdrew" or "they departed," is rendered "they returned" to pair naturally with "their own country" and to avoid a second occurrence of "go back" in the same sentence.

χρηματίζω originally belonged to the world of business and public affairs — to transact, to give a formal response, to issue an official pronouncement. In Hellenistic usage it came to mean an oracular reply from a deity, and in the New Testament the passive regularly denotes a communication from God (see also Luke 2:26; Acts 10:22; Hebrews 8:5; 11:7). The verb thus carries a sense of authoritative instruction, not merely a private impression. ἀνακάμψαι ("to bend back, return") and ἀνεχώρησαν ("they withdrew") share a subtle contrast: the road they refuse to bend back along, and the quiet retreat they make instead. The same verb ἀναχωρέω opens the next verse and recurs throughout this chapter, giving Matthew's infancy narrative a pattern of withdrawal and escape.

Dreams function in Matthew 1–2 as the ordinary channel of divine guidance, occurring five times in these two chapters. This echoes the Joseph of Genesis, a dreamer who also went down to Egypt. Notably, the magi — foreigners and astrologers from outside Israel — receive divine direction just as Joseph does, underscoring a theme Matthew develops to the end of his Gospel: the nations are drawn to Israel's Messiah. The warning also shows God working ahead of Herod, protecting the child through human obedience rather than spectacular intervention.

Herod the Great, king of Judea under Roman authority, was notorious for eliminating perceived rivals, including members of his own family. Any traveler returning through Jerusalem could reasonably be questioned, so a change of route was a real precaution as well as an act of obedience. The magi's "own country" is not specified; ancient tradition variously placed them in Persia, Babylonia, or Arabia. A return avoiding Jerusalem would likely have meant traveling south and east toward the Dead Sea before turning homeward, rather than back along the main road north.

This verse closes the Gospel reading traditionally appointed for Epiphany, the celebration of Christ's manifestation to the nations. Its final image — travelers going home changed, by a different road — has long served as a note on which the feast concludes.

text: After they had gone, suddenly an angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream and said, "Get up, take the child and his mother, and flee to Egypt. Stay there until I tell you, for Herod is about to search for the child in order to kill him."

versions.text: After they had gone, an angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream and said, "Get up, take the child and his mother, and flee to Egypt. Stay there until I tell you, for Herod is about to search for the child in order to kill him."
versions.explanation: The Greek ἰδοὺ marks a dramatic turn and is currently unrepresented. Rendering it as "suddenly" (rather than an archaic "behold") preserves the narrative jolt and reads well aloud, without disturbing the rest of the verse, which is accurate and rhythmically sound.

footnotes.text: The Greek particle ἰδού (literally "behold" or "look") is a marker of vivid surprise rather than an invitation to see something. Since "behold" now sounds archaic when read aloud, it is rendered "suddenly," which keeps the jolt of the original without stalling the sentence. The verb φαίνεται is a present tense used for a past event (a "historical present," common in narrative Greek); English narrative prefers the past, so "appeared." The participle ἐγερθείς ("having been raised up, having risen") introduces the string of commands and is best carried into English as a plain imperative, "Get up"; "Arise" is a possible but heavier alternative. The final clause ζητεῖν τὸ παιδίον τοῦ ἀπολέσαι αὐτό uses an articular infinitive of purpose, hence "in order to kill him"; ἀπολέσαι could also be rendered "destroy" or "do away with."

The chapter turns on a play of related verbs: the magi "withdrew" (ἀνεχώρησαν, v. 12), "after they had withdrawn" (Ἀναχωρησάντων, this verse), and Joseph likewise "withdrew" to Egypt (ἀνεχώρησεν, v. 14) — the same word for prudent retreat from danger binds the scenes together. μέλλει with the infinitive expresses imminent intent, "is about to," almost "is going to set about." The child is consistently called τὸ παιδίον, a diminutive for a young child, not βρέφος ("newborn"), suggesting some months have passed since the birth.

Manuscripts differ over the word order of "appears in a dream" (φαίνεται κατʼ ὄναρ versus κατʼ ὄναρ φαίνεται); the sense is identical either way, and translation cannot reflect the difference. A few witnesses also smooth the participle construction at the start of the verse. None of these variants affects the meaning.

Egypt lay outside Herod's jurisdiction as a Roman province and was the natural asylum for refugees from Judea; the journey down the coastal road would have taken roughly a week or two on foot. Egypt already held large, long-established Jewish communities, especially in Alexandria, so the family would not have been strangers among strangers. Political refugees fleeing Judean rulers for Egypt were a recognized pattern in Jewish history, and Herod's ruthlessness toward perceived rivals — including members of his own family — is well attested by ancient historians.

The flight to Egypt frames Jesus' life in the pattern of Israel's story: a tyrant who kills infants, a rescue, a sojourn in Egypt, and a coming out again (quoted from Hosea in v. 15). Many read this as presenting Jesus both as a new Moses and as embodying Israel itself. Note too that the angel says "the child and his mother," never "your son" or "your wife's son" — a careful phrasing consistent with the account of Jesus' conception, while Joseph is nonetheless entrusted with the protection of both. God's guidance comes through dreams, as with the patriarch Joseph; divine sovereignty does not remove the need for human obedience and ordinary flight.

This passage belongs to the Christmas cycle in many traditions, read near the commemoration of the infants killed by Herod and, in some calendars, on a feast of the Holy Family's flight. Coptic Christian tradition preserves a rich set of sites and observances marking the family's supposed route through Egypt.

text: So he got up, took the child and his mother during the night, and left for Egypt,

footnotes.text: The Greek opens with a participle, "and he, having been raised up / having risen," which deliberately echoes the angel's command in the previous verse ("Get up"). The translation renders it "So he got up," using "so" to make the obedience explicit for the ear: the wording of the command comes back as the wording of the action. Likewise "took the child and his mother" repeats the command's verb exactly, and the reader is meant to hear the repetition. The time phrase "during the night" stands in the Greek where it stands here, after "his mother," so the sentence keeps its original rhythm; it can attach either to the taking or to the departing, and the placement preserves that natural ambiguity. The final verb is more literally "withdrew" or "departed," but "left for Egypt" reads more smoothly aloud and lets the sentence run on into the next verse, which completes the thought with "where he stayed."

"During the night" translates a bare genitive (νυκτός), a common Greek way of expressing time within which something happens — "by night," "in the course of the night." The verb ἀναχωρέω ("withdraw, retire, take refuge") is a favourite of this Gospel and threads through the whole chapter: the Magi "withdrew" by another road, Joseph now "withdraws" to Egypt, and later he "withdraws" to Galilee. It carries the sense of a strategic retreat out of danger rather than mere travel. The participle ἐγερθείς is passive in form ("having been roused") but functions reflexively, as often with verbs of rising.

Travel by night was unusual and suggests urgency and secrecy; caravans normally moved by day. From Bethlehem the road ran south-west to the coastal highway and on across the Sinai — a journey of roughly two weeks. Egypt lay outside Herod's jurisdiction, under direct Roman administration, and had for centuries been the classic place of refuge for those fleeing rulers in the land of Israel. It also held large, long-established Jewish communities, especially in Alexandria, where a fugitive family could disappear among their own people.

The verse is presented as immediate, unquestioning obedience: no delay, no objection, not even a reported word from Joseph, who never speaks anywhere in this Gospel. The flight into Egypt also begins a pattern of correspondences the Gospel is building — a child whose life is threatened by a king, a descent into Egypt, and later a calling out of it — so that the story of the Messiah retraces the story of Israel and of Moses. God's protection here works not by spectacular rescue but through a warning dream and a father willing to act on it in the dark.
The Greek text of this verse is transmitted with remarkable stability; the manuscripts show no variation that affects the sense, only minor differences in word order and spelling in a few witnesses.

text: where he stayed until Herod's death. This was to fulfill what the Lord had said through the prophet: "Out of Egypt I called my son."

versions.text: where he stayed until Herod's death. This fulfilled what the Lord had said through the prophet: "Out of Egypt I called my son."
versions.explanation: The Greek uses a purpose clause (ἵνα πληρωθῇ, 'so that what was spoken might be fulfilled'). 'This was to fulfill' preserves that purposive sense while keeping the smooth oral rhythm; the flat 'This fulfilled' reads as a bare statement of result.

footnotes.text: The Greek begins simply "and he was there until the death of Herod." Rather than starting a new sentence, the translation joins it to the previous verse with "where he stayed," preserving the single flowing movement of flight-and-refuge that the Greek achieves with a string of connected clauses. "Until Herod's death" renders a noun phrase (literally "until the end of Herod") more naturally than the wooden "until the death of Herod." The purpose clause "in order that what was spoken might be fulfilled" is rendered "This was to fulfill what the Lord had said," which keeps the sense of divine purpose while avoiding a heavy subordinate construction that reads awkwardly aloud. Note also that the Greek carefully distinguishes two agents: the message comes *by* the Lord (the true speaker) *through* the prophet (the spokesman); the translation preserves this with "what the Lord had said through the prophet."

The word rendered "death" (teleutē) literally means "end" or "completion" and functions as a gentle euphemism, much like English "passing." The phrase "in order that it might be fulfilled" (hina plērōthē) is one of Matthew's signature formulas, appearing roughly a dozen times in his Gospel; the verb "fill full" suggests not merely prediction-and-verification but a bringing to fullness of what Scripture already contained. The quotation itself is a compact four-word line in Greek, with "out of Egypt" placed first for emphasis.

A small number of witnesses read "from the Lord" instead of "by the Lord," a difference of one preposition with no real change in meaning; the reading followed here is strongly supported. The wording of the quotation is stable across the manuscript tradition.

The quotation is from Hosea 11:1, where the words look back to the exodus and describe the nation of Israel as God's son called out of Egypt. Matthew reads the verse typologically: Jesus retraces and sums up Israel's story, going down into Egypt and being called out again, so that what was said of the people is fulfilled in the one who represents them. Notably, Matthew's wording follows the Hebrew text ("my son") rather than the common Greek version of Hosea, which reads "his children" — the singular is essential to his point. Readers have debated whether this is prediction, pattern, or both; most see here a deliberate theology of recapitulation, with Jesus as the true Israel and, in Matthew's larger framing, a new Moses who comes out of Egypt to give a new law from a mountain.

Herod the Great died in 4 BC (by the most common reckoning), at Jericho after a long and painful illness, having ordered further executions almost to the end. Egypt was a natural refuge: it lay outside Herod's jurisdiction as a Roman province, it was reachable in roughly a week or two of travel, and it hosted large, long-established Jewish communities, above all in Alexandria. Fleeing to Egypt from a hostile ruler in Judea had precedent in Israel's own history. Later Christian tradition, especially in Egypt, developed detailed itineraries of the Holy Family's journey and marked numerous sites associated with their stay.

This passage belongs to the Christmas cycle and is read in many churches on the Sunday after Christmas or in connection with the commemoration of the Holy Innocents. In the Egyptian Christian tradition the entry of the Holy Family into Egypt is kept as its own annual feast.

text: Then, when Herod realized that the wise men had outwitted him, he flew into a rage and gave orders to kill all the boys in Bethlehem and the whole surrounding region who were two years old and under, based on the time he had learned from the wise men.

versions.text: When Herod realized that the wise men had outwitted him, he flew into a rage and gave orders to kill all the boys in Bethlehem and its whole region who were two years old and under, according to the time he had learned from the wise men.
versions.explanation: Two small refinements for oral flow: "the whole surrounding region" reads more naturally aloud than "its whole region" (and renders πᾶσι τοῖς ὁρίοις αὐτῆς just as accurately), and "based on the time" avoids the ambiguity of "according to the time," which can be misheard as modifying the killing rather than Herod's calculation of the age limit. Meaning is otherwise faithful and the verse is already strong.

versions.text: When Herod realized that the wise men had outwitted him, he flew into a rage and gave orders to kill all the boys in Bethlehem and the whole surrounding region who were two years old and under, based on the time he had learned from the wise men.
versions.explanation: The opening Τότε ("then") is one of Matthew's characteristic narrative connectors, marking the shift back to Herod after the flight to Egypt. The current rendering absorbs it into "When," losing the sequential link. Adding "Then" restores the connector without disturbing the already-polished rhythm of the rest of the verse.

footnotes.text: The Greek verb ἐνεπαίχθη means "was mocked, made a fool of, tricked." "Outwitted" captures both the deception and the sting to Herod's pride; alternatives include "had tricked him," "had made a fool of him," or more literally "had mocked him." For ἐθυμώθη λίαν, literally "he was greatly enraged," the rendering "flew into a rage" preserves the force of λίαν ("exceedingly") in idiomatic English that reads aloud well. The construction ἀποστείλας ἀνεῖλεν is literally "having sent, he killed" — Herod acted through agents, so "gave orders to kill" conveys the sense rather than the wording. τοὺς παῖδας is rendered "the boys": παῖς can mean "child" generally, but the masculine plural here, together with the parallel to Pharaoh's decree, points to male children. ὁρίοις means "borders, territory," hence "the whole surrounding region." μάγοι is translated "wise men" for consistency with earlier verses in the chapter; "magi" or "astrologers" are equally defensible.

ἐνεπαίχθη is a passive form of ἐμπαίζω, built from ἐν- ("in, at") and παίζω ("to play"), literally "to play with someone" — the same verb Matthew later uses for the soldiers mocking Jesus, which quietly links Herod's humiliation to his eventual successors' scorn. There is also a sound-play in the sentence: ἐνεπαίχθη and παῖδας share the παι- syllable, so the one who was "played with" takes vengeance on "children." The phrase ἀπὸ διετοῦς καὶ κατωτέρω, "from two years old and downward," is an inclusive age bracket; διετής means "of two years," so the range covers infants up to children in their second or third year — consistent with a star sighting some months before.

Herod the Great, who died in 4 BC, was notorious for lethal suspicion toward anyone he saw as a rival: ancient historians record that he executed his wife Mariamne, her brother, her grandfather, and three of his own sons, the last just days before his own death. An order to kill infants in a village fits that character. Bethlehem was a small settlement; estimates of the number of children in the specified age range in the town and its outlying area run from a handful to a few dozen, which helps explain why an event so shocking to Bethlehem left no trace in the larger imperial record. Herod's forces also had the practical means: he maintained mercenary troops and a network of informers throughout Judea.

The episode deliberately echoes Exodus: a threatened king orders the death of Hebrew boys, and the deliverer escapes. Jesus is thus presented as a new and greater Moses, and the pattern of tyranny opposing God's chosen one runs through the whole Gospel. Interpreters have long wrestled with the deaths of the innocent here: Christian tradition honors these children as the first martyrs, dying in Christ's place though without conscious faith, and the narrative refuses to soften the fact that the coming of salvation provokes violent resistance. It also raises the question of providence — the child God protects lives, while others die — a tension Matthew leaves unresolved, moving instead to the lament of Jeremiah in the verses that follow.
The Greek text of this verse is stably transmitted across the manuscript tradition, with only trivial variation in spelling and word order among witnesses; no variant affects the meaning.

These children are commemorated as the Holy Innocents, observed on 28 December in Western tradition and on 29 December in the Byzantine calendar, with Armenian usage placing it in May. The passage is read in the Christmas season, a placement that sets the joy of the Nativity against the shadow of Herod's violence.

text: Then was fulfilled what was spoken through the prophet Jeremiah:

versions.text: Then what was spoken through the prophet Jeremiah was fulfilled:
versions.explanation: Fronting the verb keeps the sentence from stacking a long subject clause before a short verb, giving a smoother cadence for oral reading and matching the emphatic 'Then' opening. Meaning is unchanged.

footnotes.text: The Greek reads literally "what was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet, saying," placing the name before the title. English word order is reversed to "the prophet Jeremiah" because that is the natural spoken form and keeps the line moving toward the quotation that follows. The trailing participle 'saying' (legontos) is a Semitic-style quotation marker rather than a separate clause; leaving it untranslated and letting the colon do the work avoids a stiff 'saying:' before the poetry of verse 18. Note the preposition: 'through' (dia) the prophet, not 'by' him — in this Gospel's formula the words are God's, spoken by means of the prophet. 'Then was fulfilled' preserves the passive and the emphatic opening 'Then' (tote), which links the fulfillment directly to Herod's slaughter just described.

The formula 'then was fulfilled what was spoken through the prophet' is a signature refrain of this Gospel, recurring at key points in the infancy narrative and beyond. Here it appears in a shortened form: unlike other citations, it does not add 'in order that' (hina), a difference some readers take as significant — the massacre is not presented as caused by the prophecy, only as answering to it. The verb plēroō ('fill up, fulfill') carries the sense of bringing a pattern to its full measure rather than merely matching a prediction. The aorist passive ἐπληρώθη is a 'divine passive': God is the unnamed agent.

A few witnesses expand the name to 'Jeremiah' with additional qualifiers, and some early copies omit the prophet's name entirely, reading simply 'through the prophet' — likely a scribal simplification, since the surrounding fulfillment formulas often leave the prophet unnamed. The reading naming Jeremiah is strongly attested and is almost certainly original; the omission would be the easier reading. There is also minor variation in the spelling of the name.

The quotation that follows comes from Jeremiah 31:15. Interpreters differ on how the citation functions. Some read it as direct predictive prophecy fulfilled in the Bethlehem killings. Others note that in Jeremiah the verse laments the exile of the northern tribes and stands within a chapter promising restoration and a new covenant — so that by invoking it the Evangelist frames the massacre as a fresh exile-like sorrow that is nonetheless bracketed by hope. On this reading the fulfillment is typological: Israel's grief recurs, and so does God's promise of return. The passage has long been felt as one of Scripture's most honest acknowledgments that God's purposes do not cancel real grief.

Jeremiah prophesied in Jerusalem in the late seventh and early sixth centuries BC, through the Babylonian conquest and deportation. Ramah, named in the following verse, lay a few miles north of Jerusalem and served as a staging point where captives were assembled before the march to Babylon. Rachel, the ancestral mother of Joseph and Benjamin, was traditionally associated with a tomb near Bethlehem, which made the lament doubly apt for the events narrated here.

text: "A voice was heard in Ramah, weeping and loud lamentation: Rachel weeping for her children, and she would not be comforted, because they are no more."

versions.text: "A voice was heard in Ramah, weeping and loud lamentation: Rachel weeping for her children, and refusing to be comforted, because they are no more."
versions.explanation: The Greek οὐκ ἤθελεν παρακληθῆναι is a finite imperfect ("she would not be comforted"), not a participle. Rendering it as a finite clause both reflects the grammar more closely and gives the line a stronger cadence for oral reading, breaking up the string of -ing forms ("weeping... refusing").

footnotes.text: The quotation is from Jeremiah 31:15, and the wording here follows the Greek of Matthew rather than smoothing it toward the Hebrew original. "Loud lamentation" renders ὀδυρμὸς πολύς; since πολύς here signals intensity as much as quantity, alternatives include "much wailing," "bitter mourning," or "great grieving." The two nouns κλαυθμός and ὀδυρμός are kept as a pair ("weeping and loud lamentation") because the doubling itself carries the emotional weight when read aloud. "Rachel weeping for her children" supplies "for," since the Greek places τὰ τέκνα αὐτῆς directly in the accusative after the participle without a preposition. The final clause keeps the present tense of οὐκ εἰσίν — literally "they are not" — as "they are no more," which preserves the stark, unresolved note; a smoother past rendering ("because they were gone") would soften the immediacy. The verse is set in quotation marks to mark it as the prophetic citation announced in verse 17.

ὀδυρμός is a rare word in the New Testament, appearing only here and in 2 Corinthians 7:7; it denotes audible wailing rather than silent sorrow. κλαυθμός likewise names the sound of crying out, and Matthew uses it elsewhere in the phrase "weeping and gnashing of teeth." The construction κλαίουσα τὰ τέκνα αὐτῆς uses the accusative for the one lamented, a normal Greek idiom for mourning the dead. The concluding οὐκ εἰσίν is a Semitic-flavored idiom for death or disappearance — the same expression stands behind "he was not" in Genesis 5:24 and "the child is not" in Genesis 37:30.

Manuscripts differ in the placement of the verb: some read "in Ramah was heard," others "was heard in Ramah," with no difference in sense. A number of witnesses expand the line to "lamentation and weeping and wailing," a three-fold phrase drawn from the Greek version of Jeremiah; the shorter two-fold reading is generally judged original, the longer one arising from assimilation to the familiar Greek text of the prophet. Matthew's citation as a whole stands closer to the Hebrew of Jeremiah than to the common Greek version, which suggests independent rendering.

Ramah was a town in the territory of Benjamin, a few miles north of Jerusalem, and it served as a staging point where captives were assembled for deportation to Babylon (Jeremiah 40:1) — hence the cry of mourning in Jeremiah's oracle. Rachel, the beloved wife of Jacob, was the mother of Joseph and Benjamin and is here the archetypal mother of the nation weeping over her lost descendants. Two traditions located her grave: one near Bethlehem (Genesis 35:19), the other in Benjamin near Ramah (1 Samuel 10:2), and both associations serve the connection Matthew draws between the exile and the slaughter of children around Bethlehem.

Matthew reads the massacre at Bethlehem as a fresh enactment of Israel's deepest grief: what happened at the exile happens again around the newborn king. Notably, the lament he quotes stands in a chapter of promise — in Jeremiah 31:16-17 God tells Rachel to dry her tears because her children will return, and a few verses later comes the promise of a new covenant. Readers have long seen that Matthew, by citing the lament, invokes the whole context of hope surrounding it: the mourning is real, yet it is framed by restoration. The passage has therefore been central to Christian reflection on innocent suffering, on God's presence in grief that refuses easy comfort, and on the costliness of the coming of the kingdom.

This verse is the appointed reading for the commemoration of the Holy Innocents, kept in late December in many traditions, and it belongs to the Christmas cycle rather than to a season of mourning. Its imagery of a mother lamenting her lost children has shaped hymns, carols, and laments across the centuries.

text: After Herod's death, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt

versions.text: After Herod's death, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt
versions.explanation: The Greek ἰδού ('behold/look') is left untranslated. It is a characteristic Matthean marker that heightens the narrative and, in oral reading, gives a natural pause and sense of surprise before the angel's appearance. Restoring it preserves both the sense and the rhythm; the rest of the rendering (including the open-ended clause leading into v. 20) is accurate.

footnotes.text: The Greek opens with a genitive absolute, Τελευτήσαντος δὲ τοῦ Ἡρῴδου, literally "but when Herod had died" or "Herod having died." The compact phrase "After Herod's death" preserves the sense while keeping the sentence light for reading aloud. The verb φαίνεται is a historical present, "appears" — a vivid narrative device common in Greek storytelling. English narrative convention favors the past tense here, so it is rendered "appeared"; a more literal "appears" would sound abrupt when read aloud. The word order of the Greek places "in a dream" immediately after the verb; the translation places "in a dream" before "to Joseph" to match the rhythm of the parallel dream scenes earlier in the chapter. ἰδού is kept as "behold," a marker of sudden arrival; alternatives include "look," "suddenly," or leaving it untranslated, but the word signals a turning point in the story and is worth keeping. Note also that the verse is a single unfinished clause: the angel's words follow in the next verse, so the sentence deliberately ends without closing punctuation.

τελευτάω comes from τέλος, "end, completion," so it means literally "to reach the end" — a softened, almost formal way of saying "to die," much like English "to pass away." ἄγγελος simply means "messenger," and only context marks the messenger as heavenly. The phrase κατ' ὄναρ, "in a dream," is a set idiom that appears in the New Testament only in this Gospel, where it occurs six times; ὄναρ is an indeclinable neuter noun used only in this fixed expression. "An angel of the Lord" lacks the definite article in Greek, though the phrase functions almost as a title.

Manuscripts differ in the order of the words "appears" and "in a dream," and some witnesses substitute the aorist ἐφάνη, "appeared," for the present φαίνεται — likely a scribal smoothing of the historical present. Neither variant changes the meaning of the verse.

Herod the Great died at Jericho, most probably in the spring of 4 BC, after a long and painful illness; ancient accounts describe his final years as marked by suspicion and executions within his own household. At his death his kingdom was divided among three sons — Archelaus in Judea, Herod Antipas in Galilee, and Philip in the northern territories — which explains the caution in the verses that follow. Egypt lay outside Herod's jurisdiction and hosted large, long-established Jewish communities, especially in Alexandria, making it the natural place of refuge for a Judean family in flight.

This is the fourth of the dream revelations that guide the events of this chapter, presenting God as quietly directing the family's movements while political powers rage. The pattern of a Joseph who receives divine guidance through dreams and goes down to Egypt and back deliberately recalls the patriarch Joseph. The following verse echoes the words spoken to Moses in Midian, "those who sought your life are dead," drawing the child into a figure-and-fulfillment relationship with Israel's deliverer: what happened in the nation's founding story happens again, now in one person.

text: and said, "Get up, take the child and his mother, and go to the land of Israel, for those who wanted to take the child's life are dead."

footnotes.text: The Greek says literally "those seeking the child's soul (psychē)" — a Hebrew idiom in which "soul" means the whole living person, and "to seek someone's life" means to plot their death. Rendering it word for word ("seeking the child's soul") would mislead an English ear, so the translation gives the sense, "those who wanted to take the child's life," which also reads smoothly aloud. The opening participle egertheis ("having been raised up") is not a separate action to be narrated but an idiomatic prelude to a command, exactly like English "Get up and go" — hence "Get up, take... and go" rather than "Rising, take..." The verb "are dead" translates a Greek perfect: not simply that they died, but that the danger is now over. Note also that the angel says "the child and his mother," never "your son and your wife" — the translation preserves this careful wording rather than smoothing it.

Paidion is a diminutive, "little child," the same word used throughout this chapter for Jesus; it is repeated twice in this verse, giving the sentence its rhythm and its focus. The verb tethnēkasin is plural, "they are dead," even though it was Herod alone who died. This may be a generalizing plural ("the people who were after him are gone"), or it may be drawn from the wording of the passage being echoed. The clause is joined by gar ("for"), giving the reason the return is now safe.

The angel's words are almost a quotation of what the Lord says to Moses in Midian: "Go back to Egypt, for all those who were seeking your life are dead." The wording is nearly identical in the Greek Old Testament, including the striking plural "are dead." The direction is reversed — Moses is sent into Egypt, Jesus is called out of it — but the effect is to place Jesus in the line of Moses, and indeed above him: the deliverer whom a murderous king could not destroy. Together with the earlier "Out of Egypt I called my son," this presents Jesus as reliving and fulfilling the story of Israel itself.

Herod the Great died in 4 BC at Jericho, after a long and painful illness, having executed several of his own sons in his final years. His kingdom was then divided among Archelaus, Antipas, and Philip — which is why the next verses show Joseph still needing to choose his destination carefully. The phrase "land of Israel" is unusual: it is the only occurrence in the New Testament, and it evokes the ancestral covenant territory rather than any contemporary political unit such as Judea or Galilee, reinforcing the echo of the exodus and the return to the promised land.

The wording of this verse is stable across the manuscript tradition. A few witnesses smooth or expand the final clause under the influence of the Exodus passage it echoes, but the earliest and best manuscripts support the text as translated.

This verse belongs to the readings of the Christmas season, following the Flight into Egypt and the Feast of the Holy Innocents; it is the turning point of that cycle, where exile gives way to homecoming. In art and hymnody the moment is known as the Return from Egypt, often paired with the flight as a matching image.

text: So he got up, took the child and his mother, and went to the land of Israel.

footnotes.text: The Greek repeats the angel's command almost word for word, changing only the mood of the verbs: "Get up, take... and go" becomes "he got up, took... and went." The translation deliberately keeps the same English wording as verse 20 so that a listener hears the obedience echoing the command. The connective δέ is rendered "So" rather than "But" or "And," since here it marks the expected response rather than a contrast; "So he got up" also gives the sentence a forward-moving rhythm when read aloud. The verb behind "went to" more literally means "entered" or "came into," but "entered the land of Israel" would sound stiff and legal in English, and "went" preserves the plain narrative pace.

The phrase translated "got up" is an aorist participle (ἐγερθείς), literally "having been raised/roused." In Greek narrative such a participle often functions as little more than a signal that action follows — Semitic storytelling style, familiar from the Hebrew idiom "he arose and...". Note the fine distinction between παράλαβε (imperative, verse 20) and παρέλαβε (indicative, verse 21): a single vowel marks the shift from command to compliance, a pattern Matthew uses repeatedly in this chapter.

Manuscripts differ on the verb of motion: some read εἰσῆλθεν ("entered, went into"), while a large body of witnesses has ἦλθεν ("came, went"). The difference in meaning is slight, and the variant may have arisen because the simple verb sounded more natural, or conversely because the compound matched the following preposition εἰς. The rendering "went to" is compatible with either reading.

"The land of Israel" (γῆ Ἰσραήλ) occurs only here in the New Testament. It is not the ordinary political label of the first century — under Roman administration one spoke of Judea, Galilee, Samaria — but an older, covenantal name for the whole promised territory. Using it here frames the family's return as a homecoming to the land of the promise rather than a move to a Roman province.

The wording closely follows the account of Moses returning to Egypt after those who sought his life had died, taking his wife and children with him. Matthew thereby presents Jesus as the greater Moses: the child who comes out of Egypt to lead his people. The unhesitating obedience of Joseph — command and compliance in matching words — also models the righteous responsiveness to God's word that Matthew commends throughout his gospel.

text: But when he heard that Archelaus was reigning over Judea in place of his father Herod, he was afraid to go there. And after being warned in a dream, he withdrew to the region of Galilee,

versions.text: But when he heard that Archelaus was reigning over Judea in place of his father Herod, he was afraid to go there. And after being warned in a dream, he withdrew to the region of Galilee
versions.explanation: The sentence continues into the next verse ("and settled in a town called Nazareth"), so the verse should end with a comma rather than no punctuation. This also aids the reader's pacing when read aloud.

footnotes.text: The Greek uses the present tense ("Archelaus is reigning"), a vivid "historic present" that reports the news as Joseph heard it; English idiom calls for the past, "was reigning." The verb βασιλεύω properly means "to be king," and it is rendered "reigning" here because Archelaus was never actually granted the title of king — Rome made him ethnarch — so the wording reflects common speech rather than official rank. "After being warned in a dream" translates χρηματισθεὶς κατ' ὄναρ; the verb χρηματίζω means to be given an authoritative divine communication, so alternatives include "being divinely instructed," "being told by God," or "receiving an oracle." "Warned" was chosen because the context is danger and flight, and because it reads smoothly aloud. "Withdrew" keeps the guarded, tactical sense of ἀνεχώρησεν; "went away" or "retired" are possible but flatter. Literally the last phrase is "to the parts of Galilee" (τὰ μέρη), an idiom for a territory or district, here simply "the region of Galilee."

βασιλεύω here takes the genitive τῆς Ἰουδαίας, an older construction meaning "to be king over" a territory; elsewhere the New Testament prefers βασιλεύω with ἐπί plus a case. The passive χρηματισθείς belongs to a family of words built on χρῆμα ("matter, business"): the active verb can mean "to transact business" or "to bear a name," but in religious usage it means to deliver or receive an oracle — hence the passive, "having been given divine direction." Note also that ἀνεχώρησεν is one of Matthew's signature verbs (used of the magi in 2:12, of Joseph in 2:14, and later of Jesus repeatedly), tying this escape into a pattern of withdrawal from threat.

Archelaus, a son of Herod the Great by his Samaritan wife Malthace, received Judea, Samaria, and Idumea when his father's kingdom was divided in 4 BC. Augustus withheld the title "king" and made him ethnarch. Early in his rule he had thousands of pilgrims killed in the temple courts at Passover, and his misgovernment led to his deposition and exile to Gaul around AD 6, after which Judea came under Roman prefects. Galilee, by contrast, fell to his brother Herod Antipas — a separate jurisdiction and, at that moment, the safer choice. This detail places the family's resettlement in the north within a precise and verifiable political situation.

There are minor variants in the manuscripts: some copies add the article before "Archelaus," some give the infinitive form of the verb ("that Archelaus was to reign"), and the phrase naming Herod appears in differing word orders ("his father Herod" / "Herod his father"). A few witnesses also insert "the king" alongside Herod's name. None of these readings changes the sense of the verse, and the text followed here is well supported by the earliest witnesses.

This is the fourth dream in Matthew's opening chapters, but unlike the earlier ones no angel is named — the divine initiative alone is stressed. The passage holds together two things Christians have often separated: Joseph's genuine fear of a violent ruler and his obedience to God's guidance. Providence does not remove the danger; it directs a path through it.
