Matthew also quietly prepares the reader for a Messiah shaped by Galilee rather than Jerusalem, an obscurity that will later be used against Jesus but which the evangelist presents as the fulfillment of prophecy in the next verse.

text: and he came and settled in a town called Nazareth, so that what was spoken through the prophets might be fulfilled: "He will be called a Nazarene."

versions.text: and settled in a town called Nazareth, so that what was spoken through the prophets might be fulfilled: "He will be called a Nazarene."
versions.explanation: The participle ἐλθών ("having come") is left untranslated. Restoring "he came and settled" reflects the Greek and gives the clause a fuller rhythm for oral reading, matching the narrative movement from the previous verse's "he withdrew to the region of Galilee."

footnotes.text: The Greek reads literally "settled into a town," using a verb of dwelling with a preposition of motion; English idiom requires "came and settled in." The clause "so that what was spoken through the prophets might be fulfilled" renders a purpose construction that Matthew uses repeatedly in these opening chapters. Note that he writes "spoken through the prophets" (plural) rather than his usual "written by the prophet" (singular), so the introduction is deliberately general and no single quoted passage is named; the wording has therefore been kept broad rather than smoothed into a citation formula. The final word, Nazōraios, is rendered "Nazarene" — an inhabitant of Nazareth — though it could also be transliterated "Nazorean" to preserve the unusual spelling, since the term later functioned almost as a title (compare its use in the inscription on the cross and as a name for Jesus' followers).

Nazōraios is a slightly odd formation; the more expected adjective from "Nazareth" would be Nazarēnos, which other Gospel writers use. The unusual vowel has long suggested to interpreters that Matthew is exploiting a play on sound. Two Hebrew words are most often proposed: netser, "shoot" or "branch" (Isaiah 11:1, "a shoot from the stump of Jesse"), and nazir, "one consecrated," the word used of Samson, who is announced before birth and called holy to God. Hebrew wordplay of this kind, linking a name to a prophetic word by consonantal echo rather than by exact quotation, is well attested in Jewish interpretation of the period.

Nazareth was a small agricultural village in lower Galilee, home perhaps to a few hundred people, set on a ridge a short walk from the larger Hellenized city of Sepphoris. It is never mentioned in the Hebrew Scriptures, nor in early Jewish histories, and its obscurity lies behind the later question whether anything good could come from there. Archaeology shows terraced farming, wine and olive presses, cisterns and rock-cut tombs — the setting of an ordinary working village. Galilee was under the rule of Herod Antipas rather than Archelaus, which is why it offered the family relative safety.

The verse completes the chain of "fulfilments" that has carried the family from Bethlehem to Egypt and now to Galilee, and it grounds the name by which Jesus would be known throughout his ministry. Interpreters differ on what prophecy is meant: some hear Isaiah's promise of the messianic "branch" from David's line, so that the village name secretly announces royal descent; others hear the theme of one set apart and consecrated to God from the womb; still others take the plural "prophets" to point to the general prophetic expectation that the Messiah would be despised and from a place of no reputation. On any reading the point is that God's purpose is served precisely through obscurity: the Messiah is identified not by a famous city but by a village nobody expected.

The place name is spelled variously in the manuscripts — Nazaret, Nazareth, and Nazara — with no difference in meaning; the form ending in -t has good early support. Some witnesses read the plural "prophets" while a few give the singular "prophet," evidently an attempt to make the citation formula match Matthew's usual pattern; the plural is the better attested and harder reading.
